items.q: Task Scheduler — minimum intervals with a cooldown
shortAnswer: Return the minimum time units to run all tasks, where the same task must wait `n` units between runs.
The most frequent task dictates the skeleton: `(max - 1) * (n + 1) + tasksWithMaxCount`, then clamp to `tasks.size`.
The clamp is the detail that separates memorizing from understanding — when no idle is needed, extra tasks just extend the frame. Time O(tasks).
items.prompt:
Given `tasks: CharArray` and a cooldown `n`, each unit of CPU can process one task (or idle). The same task must wait `n` units between runs. Return the minimum number of time units to complete all tasks.

The greedy insight: the most frequent task dictates the skeleton — arrange it with `n` gaps, then fill the gaps with other tasks. The formula `(maxCount - 1) * (n + 1) + numberWithMax` is the classic answer, with the caveat that it's only valid when no task exceeds the gaps.
hints: Which task constrains the schedule the most? The most frequent one.
If task A appears 3 times with cooldown 2, the skeleton is A _ _ A _ _ A. What fills the blanks?
Formula: `(max-1)*(n+1) + tasksWithMaxCount`, but clamp to `tasks.size` — extra tasks just extend the frame. Verify the clamp with an example where n is small.

code.caption: Greedy formula — O(tasks)

items.complexity: Time O(tasks) to count, O(26) to scan. Space O(1) (fixed alphabet). The `maxOf(frame, tasks.size)` clamp is the detail that separates a memorized formula from an understood one.
followUps: When is the formula wrong? (When idle never appears — that's what the clamp handles.)
Return the actual schedule, not just the length (needs a max-heap simulation).
What if tasks have weights / different priorities?

items.q: Coin Change — fewest coins to reach an amount
shortAnswer: Return the fewest coins to make an amount with unlimited denominations, or -1 if impossible.
Bottom-up DP: `dp[a] = min(dp[a - c] + 1)` over coins at most `a`, seeding `dp[0] = 0` and everything else to a sentinel.
Greedy fails — (1, 3, 4) for amount 6 is the counterexample. The sentinel tells impossible from possible; O(amount × coins) time.
items.prompt:
Given coin denominations `coins: IntArray` (unlimited supply) and an amount, return the fewest number of coins to make that amount, or -1 if impossible.

The 1D DP classic: `dp[a]` = fewest coins for amount a, built bottom-up from the denominations. Interviewers will also expect you to know the greedy is wrong (25,10,5,1 works; 1,3,4 and amount 6 doesn't).
hints: Greedy fails for some denomination sets — find a counterexample (1, 3, 4 → 6). That's why this needs DP.
Define `dp[a] = min(dp[a-c] + 1)` over all coins c ≤ a. Build from 1 to amount.
Seed `dp[0] = 0` and everything else to a large sentinel. If `dp[amount]` is still the sentinel, return -1.

code.caption: Bottom-up 1D — O(amount × coins)

items.complexity: Time O(amount × coins), space O(amount). The sentinel `amount + 1` is legal because you can never need more than `amount` coins (all 1s) when it's possible.
followUps: Why does greedy fail? Give the (1,3,4)→6 counterexample.
Count the *number of ways* (unbounded knapsack counting) instead of the minimum.
What if each coin may be used once? (0/1 knapsack variant.)

shortAnswer: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, preserving original element order.
The O(n²) DP extends the best previous chain; the upgrade keeps `tails[k]`, the smallest tail of each length, via binary search.
`tails` holds lengths, not the subsequence — reconstructing needs parent pointers. State the O(n²) answer first, then upgrade.
items.prompt:
Given `nums: IntArray`, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (elements keep their order but need not be contiguous).

The O(n²) DP is `dp[i] = max(dp[j]) + 1` over j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]. The O(n log n) version maintains a patience-sorting pile — the interviewer will ask for it as the follow-up. You should be able to do both.
hints: The naive O(n²): for each i, look back at all j < i and extend the best chain that ends lower.
State: `dp[i]` = LIS length ending exactly at i. Answer = max over all i.
O(n log n): keep `tails[k]` = smallest tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. Binary-search where the new number belongs and overwrite.

code.caption: Patience sorting — O(n log n)

items.complexity: Time O(n log n) with binary search, space O(n). The O(n²) DP is the simpler first answer — state it, then upgrade. Note `tails` is *not* the actual subsequence, just the lengths.
followUps: Reconstruct the actual subsequence — why does plain `tails` not hold it? (You need parent pointers.)
Number of increasing subsequences, not just the length.
Longest *non-decreasing* — flip `<` to `<=` and re-examine the binary search.

items.q: 0/1 Knapsack — max value within a capacity
shortAnswer: Return the maximum value carried within a capacity, with each item usable at most once.
One-dimensional DP over capacity, with take-or-skip transitions, iterating capacity backward so each item is used at most once.
The backward direction is mandatory — a forward loop silently turns 0/1 into unbounded knapsack. Time O(n·W), space O(W).
items.prompt:
Given weights and values for n items (each usable at most once) and a capacity, return the maximum total value you can carry.

The template behind 'subset sum', 'partition equal subset', and 'target sum'. The state is `dp[i][c]` = best value using the first i items and capacity c. The transition is the real lesson: take vs skip.
hints: Two dimensions: items considered and capacity. `dp[i][c]` = max value from the first i items within capacity c.
For item i: either skip it (`dp[i-1][c]`) or take it (`value[i] + dp[i-1][c-weight[i]]`) if it fits. Take the max.
Space-optimize to one array iterating capacity *backward* — backward is mandatory so each item is used at most once.

code.caption: 1D backward loop — O(n·W)

items.complexity: Time O(n·W), space O(W) with the optimized 1D array. The backward iteration direction is the subtle bit — forward would let an item be reused, turning 0/1 into unbounded.
followUps: Why must the 1D loop go backward? What breaks if it's forward?
Subset-sum: is a subset summing exactly to target possible? Same engine with values = weights.
Recover *which* items were chosen (parent pointers or bitset).

shortAnswer: Count the distinct paths from top-left to bottom-right of an m×n grid, moving only right or down.
Grid DP where each cell sums its top and left neighbors, with the first row and column seeded to 1.
The closed form is `C(m+n-2, m-1)` — name it, then code the grid. O(m·n) time, space reducible to one row.
items.prompt:
A robot starts at the top-left of an m×n grid and can only move right or down. Return the number of distinct paths to the bottom-right.

Warm-up combinatorial/DP problem. Two valid answers: pure combinatorics `C(m+n-2, m-1)`, or the DP grid where each cell sums its top and left neighbors. The DP recurrence is the pattern that generalizes to obstacles and weighted cells.
hints: To reach cell (r,c) you must come from (r-1,c) or (r,c-1). Counts add.
`dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]`, with the top row and left column seeded to 1.
The combinatorial answer is `choose(m+n-2, m-1)` — mention it as a closed-form alternative, then code the grid.

code.caption: 2D grid DP — O(m·n)

items.complexity: Time O(m·n), space O(m·n) (reducible to O(min(m,n)) by keeping one row). The closed form is O(m+n) with big-int care.
followUps: Add obstacles — cells with a 1 you cannot enter; how does the seed row change?
Reduce space to one row. Which direction must you sweep?
Minimum path sum with weighted cells — same grid, different recurrence.

shortAnswer: Return the longest substring of a string that reads the same forward and backward.
Expand around every center — single characters for odd lengths and the gaps between for even — tracking the best start and length.
Track start and length rather than materializing substrings, keeping space O(1). Time O(n²); name Manacher's O(n) as the extra.
items.prompt:
Given a string, return the longest palindromic substring.

Two classic answers: expand around centers (O(n²) time, O(1) space — simplest, interviewers love it) and Manacher's (O(n), usually an extra). You should code the center-expansion fluently and be able to explain why it's O(n²) with n centers each expanding O(n).
hints: A palindrome is symmetric around a center. Every palindrome has a center — either a single char (odd length) or between two chars (even).
There are 2n-1 centers. For each, expand outward while the ends match and track the longest run.
Keep track of the best start/length rather than materializing each substring — O(1) extra space.

code.caption: Expand around centers — O(n²) time, O(1) space

items.complexity: Time O(n²) — n·2 centers, each expanding to O(n). Space O(1). Manacher's is O(n) but fiddly; naming it and its complexity is usually enough at interview depth.
followUps: Why is there no O(n) *space* version needed here? (We never store the DP table.)
Count all palindromic substrings — same expansion, count instead of max.
When would you reach for Manacher's over this?

items.q: Design a Rate Limiter (fixed window and token bucket)
shortAnswer: Design a rate limiter allowing at most N requests per window W per key.
Fixed window stores each key's window start and count; token bucket stores tokens and last refill, adding `elapsed × rate` capped at capacity.
Name the weakness: fixed windows allow a 2N boundary burst; the token bucket smooths it. O(1) per call, with eviction for many keys.
items.prompt:
Design a `RateLimiter` that allows at most N requests per time window W. Support `allow(key: String, nowMs: Long): Boolean`.

Two implementations matter: fixed window (a map key → window start + count) and token bucket (key → tokens + last refill time). Know both and say when each is right — fixed window is simpler and has boundary spikes; token bucket smooths bursts. On Android this is the shape of a throttling layer in front of an API client.
hints: Start simple: `HashMap<Key, WindowState>` where WindowState = (windowStart, count). Reset when nowMs passes the window edge.
Fixed window allows a 2N burst across a boundary — name that weakness out loud.
Token bucket: store tokens and lastRefill; on each call, add (now-last)/rate tokens, cap at capacity, allow if tokens >= 1.

code.caption: Token bucket — smooth, burst-tolerant

items.complexity: Time O(1) per call with a map lookup. Space O(keys). Both windows degrade gracefully; fixed window is one `if` simpler. Cleanup of idle keys (LRU eviction) is a production concern to mention.
followUps: Fixed window boundary burst — how would you eliminate it? (Sliding log or token bucket.)
What happens with 10k distinct keys? (Map grows — add eviction.)
How would you do this across multiple processes? (Shared store with a lock/atomic op.)
